institutionName: Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was in Brazil traveling a bit around 5 years ago and just loved the way people approached me. But the country is so complex that I knew I was only scraping a surface and got curious to get to know Brazil with all of its joys and problems.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I give it a 10 now, not in the sense that I was happy all the time but in the sense that I really got challenged personally and learned a lot. Rio is lovely and I'm really happy that I went.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: From KU's side it was quite organized and even though there are some things you need to keep check of when traveling outside of Europe travel wise where you're more on your own, I was emailed about all deadlines regarding university stuff and also got informed on the essential visa things. Information flow from Brazil was quite slow but I got to learn when I got there that they're equally flexible and it's about keeping a cool mind

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We got some emails from an intro group for exchange students with meet up dates and stuff. Unfortunately I was misinformed by more official sites of UFRJ about the semester start which made the beginning very chaotic because, in addition to it all being in portuguese, I started my courses 3 lectures late and it therefore took some extra time to get into what the courses were all about. But when I found out that something was wrong, a random professor who just happened to be nearby took an hour out of his day just to help me without me even asking.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The international office was really not very helpful but everybody else was just amazing to help me fix my situation.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I found a room on
webquarto.com.br
. Really easy and people there tend to move with only few days' notice so you don't have to find anything very well in advance. I did, but ended up moving 3 months later.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of bad apartments in Rio and some family houses with strange rules so it's good to do your research. However, if you really want to dive into the culture and learn the language, I would  avoid the safe option of living with other exchange students. I lived with Brazilians and got a great deal out of it both experience, language and culture wise.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I don't have too much of an opinion about this one because I knew that there wouldn't be help to find housing and it's not very hard for a European to find affordable housing in Rio due to currency differences.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very free and flexible but you have to double check that everything is alright because they don't inform you if it's not.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Well as mentioned, I was misinformed about the date of the university start. Long story short, the bachelor degree's semester start was delayed due to political issues and I was informed by the international office of UFRJ that mine was too, although it wasn't the case for the master's degree. So I came to the office mildly panicing about if it was even possible to be registered 2 weeks late. But I just had to ask the professors if I could join, and if they were cool with it, there was no issue.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The master's degree administration office were quite helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very unsuccesful haha, the 2 classes I signed up for at home were not offered so I had to sign up for some others. But it all worked out.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't think too much about the courses in advance because they do change some things that's impossible to figure out online and it all works out as you get there. And arrive early and go to the campus administration office to get some information before semester start because things work quite differently. And most importantly, know some Portuguese before you arrive, I would've been really stressed if I had been a complete beginner. The more you can communicate, the softer you'll land cause most of them really do not speak English at all.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I am an economics student and took courses in a cross disciplinary field of "International Political Economics" so I was often in doubt how much of the culture shock came from being in a different country and how much came from studying a different field.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was quite difficult to follow the lectures in the beginning due to the language barrier. I was about intermediate when I started but daily Portuguese and academic Portuguese are quite different so it takes a little time to get into it. But had it been my first language I think I'd have been just fine.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was smaller classes and a mix of lecture and class discussion all in one. They're not so clear on when class starts and ends and when we have breaks and stuff so I could sometimes miss the degree of structure from at home but my professors were quite enthusiastic about their classes and their academic views are really different from some of the mainstream opinions at home so I learned a lot from having contested some views I just took for granted.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
EPI701 Economia Política Internacional I (taught by Mauricio Metri)
EPI738 Economia Política do Desenvolvimento da China (taught by Isabela Nogueira)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I'd recommend both. The courses are part of a course series and wouldn't necessarily be exactly the same but I really liked the professors and learned a lot from the content because they have a completely different discourse on both geopolitics and China. I mention the professors as an important factor because not all professors at the university are equally good and with the flexible teaching style that matters even more than in DK.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I was warned that I'd end up taking the Uber a lot but it was more true than I'd expected. I didn't feel comfortable taking the metro after 8-9pm on weekdays so if I wanted to go somewhere, I'd very often go with an Uber. It's really cheap but it adds up.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing was cheaper than I expected. I lived quite well in a big place in a somewhat safe neighborhood for less money than I'd pay at home. It's worth the extra 500 reais a month to live in Zona Sul.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university itself has some social offers (dance classes and other fun classes, as well as sports teams that are quite competitive) that I didn't take part in because it was at the main campus in the north part of town and I was at the social sciences campus in the south, almost an hour away. But Rio just has so much to offer and people are so open, so if you have a hobby, go find somewhere to do it and you'll most certainly meet people if you're open too.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Show up for the intro days for the exchange students!!! I wanted to try mostly being with brazilians but it's just so nice to still have a network of people who also want to go explore. And Interpoli (the exchange welcoming program) has a lot of Brazilians so often we would end up being 50/50 brazilians/foreigners when we met up and still speak mostly Portuguese.

Hobby wise, I didn't do anything that had to do with uni but danced a lot of forró and went hiking every week. Rio has a lot of mountains and they're really easy to get to when you're over the firste time's hurdles, and I really enjoyed that. And everything goes on by Instagram, I'd have liked to know that earlier. E.g. if you wanna find places to dance, sites like "forronorio" tell you exactly where you can go do that every single day.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Every single mountain top of Rio itself :) E.g. Bico do Papagayo, Morro dos Dois Irmãos and Pedra da Gavea are really nice. If you have a lot of time off at some point, Salvador and Chapada Diamantina in Bahia are lovely.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was not my first time in Brazil so I had an idea of what I was getting myself into. And people are just so nice that it was easy most of the time. There were culture shocks along the way but I'd have been disappointed if it had all been easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be open and start some conversations. And patient. I only figured out I had a lot in common with a few of my classmates about a month into the course.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Their very high tolerance to noise, e.g. loud music in the living room and such. And those mini cultural codes where I had no chance of knowing that I was being unintentionally strange or impolite in their eyes until someone luckily told me.
And that people didn't trust each other and some therefore also didn't make an effort to be trustable. It is true that you have to be a bit less naive on the streets of Rio than in Cph.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their openness, their friendliness and curiosity, especially to foreigners, how easy it was to get to know people, how some would spend their time helping a stranger out without having to at all, and their latin american charm :)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) I hope you'll love it as much as I did
2) I'll highly advise you to prioritize learning Portuguese in advance, it'll mean a lot to how easily you'll get into the culture and how fast you'll start making Brazilian friends
3) Don't forget to research on and exploit all the city has to offer. Cause it really is a lot.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I got stressed about the practicalities before going because I only had the last information needed for e.g. my visa quite last minute. But somehow they always make it all work out. Get a hang of the visa application process and also start quite well in advance cause you'll have to go to the embassy a few times.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I did have a great time in Rio, but the most rewarding part of it all was actually all the bumps on the way. And the new friends who made me get through it, and getting fluent in a new language as a direct product of all the bumps on the way :)

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I arrived well before study start which was great to get a hang of the language. But being a month on "vacation" in a new city where you don't know anyone, nor where to go to get to know new people, can be quite lonely. So the first month was a bit long.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: It's all much less scary as soon as you get there :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
